questions.title: Why is NormalFloat (“NF_k”) claimed to be information‑theoretically optimal?
questions.question_body:
The paper states that NormalFloat achieves an "information theoretically optimal" data type for zero‑centered normally distributed weights whose bins contain an equal number of elements. What exactly does "information theoretically optimal" mean here? Is it merely minimising mean squared error while enforcing equiprobable bins, or does it involve entropy maximisation / KL divergence minimisation? Also:
  • How does Vanishing Zero represent express accurate zeros during training?
  • Compared with plain Integer/Float (IEEE FP/Int), what practical advantages arise from this construction?

questions.title: How do you construct an asymmetric NF_k data type so it contains a discrete zero point?
questions.question_body:
The text explains creating an asymmetric datatype consisting of two ranges – one negative side with 2^(k−1) cells and one positive side with 2^(k−1)+1 cells – then removing duplicate zeros. Could someone detail the mathematical steps:
  • Approximate‐to zero placement?
  • When computing q_i =½(Q_X(i/(2^k+1))+Q_X((i+1)/(2^k+1))), how do you merge the two halves?
And how large is the discretisation error introduced compared with symmetric schemes?

questions.title: (Double Quantisation) How does saving bytes for scale parameters actually work?
questions.question_body:
“Double Quantisation” replaces every original floating‑point scale constant (c_2^{FP32}) by a secondary compressed representation living in FP8 followed finally by an additional constant (c_1^{FP32}).
A few points caused confusion:
  • What mathematical operation creates c_2scaled? Does it subtract its own mean before symmetric grouping?
  • Using block sizes B=64 for W and 256 for c_2 gives an average saving ≈ 0 Φ733 bits per parameter according the paper—can you walk through that calculation?
  • Finally why do we need a second‐level constant c_1^{FP32}? Isn’t c_2 already sufficient?

questions.title: "DoubleDeQuant": why apply de‐arith twice instead of once?
questions.question_body:
“DoubleDeQuant” repeatedly calls "dequant": X = dequant( dequant(c_1^{FP32},c_2^{k-bit}), W ) My understanding:
  • The first "dequant" expands c_2 from its compressed FP8 format into an exact FP32 scaling factor for its block.
  • The second slices W’s stored k‑bit codes (under their own per‐block scales generated in first step) and returns a BF16 tensor.
What gains come from doing two stages instead of directly rescaling W through its native k‐bit op? Does this allow keeping blocks’ multiples aligned conveniently whatever their sizes were?

questions.title: Why must LoRA adapters live in *every* Transformer layer rather than only query/value projections?
questions.question_body:
Experiments reported significant accuracy loss when only inserting adapters into query/value projections.
  • Is there a theoretical reason—e.g. in broader expressive capacity—that mandates inserting here?
  • Do modern feeding network structures impose representational bottlenecks otherwise?
  • Could enlarging the adapter rank compensate for fewer layers?
    one experiment found rank change negligible compared against adapter count.

questions.title: Rank r seems almost irrelevant—why?
questions.question_body:
Figure shown indicates varying r has tiny effect (<0 % change) once total adapter quantity reaches sufficiency.
  • From a expressiveness perspective Landau‐style argument how many singular vectors suffice given residual dimension sizes?
  • Capped adapt–capacity plateau reminds me “overparameterisation” saturation—you can tune any function up-pasted via sufficient linear combinations.
    even beyond certain threshold further increasing r gives diminishing returns.

questions.title: How do Paged Optimisers prevent GPU out‑of‑memory spikes during checkpointing?
questions.question_body:
Gradient checkpointing stores activations off‑device temporarily when processing very long sequences.
actionable bonus mentioned involves NVIDIA unified memory paging
and later reloading during optimiser updates.
also dubious calibration  specifically:
  • Which tensors trigger page faults – optimizer states/g_roads—or activation buffers?
    eliminate ghost spikes—for batch/seqlength specific settings outlined.

questions.title: Is freezing base weights during backprop sufficient to prevent drift among other gradients?
questions.question_body:
The procedure computes gradients through frozen tensors f(x)=W·x→ calls “freezing” W while computing ∂L/∂W unlike regular SGD.
author’s claim tests assert updates applied exclusively to LoRAs. nice question:
  • If accumulation occurs anywhere through autograd dynamical graph – can cached gradients still get written back inadvertently?

questions.\u201CGPT\u201D auto‑evaluation bias: The authors observe GPT-GOM four consistently awards higher scores when its response appears first. their suggested solution is averaging scores over order permutations. but: lazy me wonder : Is there rigourous proof based on greedy ranking function that proves swapping order necessarily skews scoring, or merely empirical observation?
